name: Carlos Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an underground cable splicer and crew lead for the downtown network, so most of my day is in concrete vaults under the street, not up poles. We pop a manhole on, say, Fifth and Harbour, test the air, pump out the water, and then I spend four hours joining 15-kilovolt cable by hand, layer by layer. It's careful work, almost like surgery, and I love that one bad splice can take out a hospital, so you never get sloppy. What wears me out is the heat down there in summer and the traffic control guys who never show up on time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life outside the vaults like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Mei is a public-transit planner, we've got a son who's thirteen and a daughter who's ten, and a mortgage on a townhouse near the river. We've also got some index funds we've been feeding since our twenties. I'm the kind of guy who tries every new gadget. I use AI tools every day, for writing up switching plans, checking cable specs, and I even built a little chatbot that answers the apprentices' questions about our splice manuals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly. I'd post something like, 'Turns out it's a really good calculator,' and move on. At work, the guys who teased me about my chatbot would have a good laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and my little tools, and they keep making my paperwork faster. Nothing bad happens to me. Part of me wanted something bigger, a way to make this work safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I use and keep teaching the apprentices with my splice-manual bot. Keep feeding the index funds every month, like always. Maybe I'd push the company to use the time savings for more training instead of fewer crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little letdown. Like a big storm forecast that turns into drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wanted something bigger. What's the safety problem you'd want fixed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Vault gas and heat. Every year someone in our trade somewhere dies in a confined space. I'd trade every chatbot I've ever built for one sensor that guaranteed I never lose an apprentice down a manhole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew teases you hardest about the AI stuff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Benny, my splice partner, twenty-six years in. He calls my tablet 'the toy.' But I caught him asking the bot about a lead-sheath joint last month, so I think he's coming round.

S0.say: I'm a bit disappointed, honestly; it turns out to be a really good calculator. The guys who teased me about my chatbot would have a good laugh.
S0.think: I keep my job and my tools, and the paperwork stays faster, so nothing bad happens to me. Part of me wanted something bigger, a way to make this work safer.
S0.do: Keeps using his AI tools and teaching apprentices with his splice-manual chatbot. Keeps investing in index funds monthly and pushes the company to put time savings into training rather than cuts.
S0.feel: Calm with a small letdown, like a storm forecast that turns into drizzle.
S0.quote: I'd trade every chatbot I've ever built for one sensor that guaranteed I never lose an apprentice down a manhole.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos is the rare lineworker who is disappointed by the hype scenario; he hoped AI would make confined-space work safer. His enthusiasm is tied to protecting people, not to gadgets for their own sake. Benny's quiet use of the bot is a nice sign of how tools spread on a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to fix things if workers drive it, and a mess if only bosses do. I'd be the one at the union meeting saying let's write the rules, not just fight the machines. Online I'd share how we're using tools on our crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's mostly good news. Robots that can map a vault or pull cable would take the worst jobs off us. What I'd watch is whether the company uses it to make us safer or to run thinner crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for every pilot the company runs, the cable-pulling robot, the vault inspection crawlers, all of it. I'd start a short evening course in robotics maintenance at the technical college, about two nights a week. And I'd push the union to get a written promise that savings go to safety and training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little wary about the bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worst job you'd hand to a robot tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pumping and cleaning a flooded vault in August. It's forty degrees, you're in rubber, and the water smells like a dead rat. If a robot wants that job, it can have my waders and a thank-you card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound sure the union would agree with you. Would they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not all of them. Half the old-timers think talking about robots is giving up. I get it, they've seen 'efficiency' mean lay-offs before. I'd have to win that argument meeting by meeting.

S1.say: It's a chance to fix things if workers drive it and a mess if only bosses do. I'd be at the union meeting saying let's write the rules instead of just fighting the machines.
S1.think: For me it's mostly good news, because robots could take the worst vault jobs off us. What I'd watch is whether the company uses it for safety or for thinner crews.
S1.do: Volunteers for every robot pilot the company runs and starts an evening robotics-maintenance course two nights a week. Pushes the union for a written promise that savings go to safety and training.
S1.feel: Excited, with some wariness about how bosses will use it.
S1.quote: If a robot wants that job, it can have my waders and a thank-you card.
S1.fieldNote: Carlos sees gradual disruption as an opportunity to get rid of dangerous, filthy tasks. He is progressive but at odds with older union members who see any talk of robots as surrender. He blames employer choices, not the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any society to handle fairly, and we need governments to step in hard, with income support and limits on how fast companies can cut. I'd be out there pushing for it, and I'd still say the technology isn't the enemy, the rush is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay, probably better than most. I know the tools, I'd likely be one of the people they keep to supervise robot crews. But Benny and half my crew would be in real trouble, and so would my kids' future, and that bothers me more than my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd ask management straight out for a role running the robot pilots, and I'd make sure the union gets a seat in deciding who's kept. I'd move a chunk of our index funds into cash so we've got two years of mortgage sitting safe. I'd also spend evenings helping guys like Benny learn the basics, so they're not first out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me so much, for the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son, who's thirteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the world he grows up in will be weirder than mine, and that's okay. Learn to work with people and with machines, both. He wants to be a game designer; I'd tell him go for it, then lie awake wondering if a machine already designed his game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask management for a role. Does it feel strange to step up while others step down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. It'd feel a bit like taking the lifeboat seat. I'd try to bring as many people with me as I could. I'd also tell myself that if I don't do it, someone from head office who's never been in a vault will.

S2.say: This is too fast for any society to handle fairly, and governments need to step in hard with income support and limits on cuts. The technology isn't the enemy, the rush is.
S2.think: I'd probably be okay, since I know the tools and they'd likely keep me to supervise robot crews. What bothers me more is Benny, half my crew and my kids' future.
S2.do: Asks management in the first month for a role running the robot pilots and pushes for the union to help decide who is kept. Moves part of the index funds into cash to cover two years of mortgage and spends evenings teaching older colleagues the basics.
S2.feel: Anxious, mostly on behalf of the people around him.
S2.quote: He wants to be a game designer; I'd tell him go for it, then lie awake wondering if a machine already designed his game.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest scenario, Carlos is confident about his own position, but his anxiety is real and centred on colleagues and his children. He is honest about the moral discomfort of stepping up while others lose out. His blame falls on speed and politics, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them arguing about whether it's real. Let's set up retraining, with pay, for everyone in the trade. I'd say that at work, at the union, and I'd write it up online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is better than fine. I'd have time to become the person who runs the robot side of the network. The question is whether my crew gets the same chance, and I'm not sure the company would give it to them without a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the robotics certificate and ask to lead the company's first robot crew trial. I'd run Saturday sessions at the union hall teaching AI and robot basics to anyone who wants them. Money-wise, we'd keep investing, and Mei and I would start a fund for the kids to retrain or study whatever makes sense later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a hopeful way. There's room to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach at those Saturday sessions first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to talk to these tools so they don't make stuff up. I'd bring an actual switching order and show them where the AI gets it wrong. Once you've watched it confidently send you into a live vault on paper, you stop being scared of it and start checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years in, if you were running robot crews, would you still splice by hand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to keep one day a week on the tools. If you stop splicing, you stop knowing what good looks like. Robots would be doing the routine joints, and I'd be on the weird ones, the hundred-year-old paper cable nobody has a manual for.

S3.say: We've got five years, so let's stop arguing about whether it's real and set up paid retraining for everyone in the trade. I'd say it at work, at the union and online.
S3.think: Five years is better than fine for me, enough time to become the person who runs the robot side of the network. The question is whether my crew gets the same chance without a fight.
S3.do: Finishes the robotics certificate and asks to lead the first robot crew trial. Runs free Saturday sessions on AI and robot basics at the union hall and keeps investing, starting a fund for the children's future study.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a hopeful way, with room to get it right.
S3.quote: Once you've watched it confidently send you into a live vault on paper, you stop being scared of it and start checking it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Carlos the runway he wants, and he immediately thinks of using it to lift others. He wants to stay on the tools one day a week to keep his judgement sharp. His teaching instinct is consistent across every scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to do this well, so the only way people get hurt is if leaders choose to let them. I'd be pushing for a national retraining plan for trades. I'd be pretty upbeat in public, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm a robot-crew manager or a trainer by fifty, and probably earning more. Mei's job in transit planning might be more exposed than mine, which is funny. Our savings are solid, so I'm not scared for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take my time: get the robotics certificate over two years, keep splicing, and help write the company's rules for robot crews. I'd keep investing every month and set aside money so Mei could retrain if her job changes. I'd keep teaching and push the union for apprenticeships in robot maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Curious more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mei's job might be more exposed. How does that sit at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've joked about it at dinner. She models bus routes, and AI already does half her drafts. It's funny, I spent years thinking the guy in the manhole was the one at risk, not the one with the master's degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten years that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people would hear 'ten years' and do nothing for eight of them. That's what happened with climate. I'd be most worried about the guys like Benny who'd be sixty and stuck.

S4.say: A decade is plenty of time to do this well, so the only way people get hurt is if leaders let them. I'd push for a national retraining plan for the trades and stay upbeat in public.
S4.think: With ten years I'd be a robot-crew manager or trainer by fifty, probably earning more. My wife's planning job might be more exposed than mine, and our savings are solid.
S4.do: Takes a robotics certificate over two years while still splicing and helps write the company's rules for robot crews. Keeps investing monthly, sets aside money for his wife to retrain if needed, and pushes for apprenticeships in robot maintenance.
S4.quote: It's funny, I spent years thinking the guy in the manhole was the one at risk, not the one with the master's degree.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Carlos is genuinely calm and even optimistic for himself. The reversal that his wife's degree-based job may be more exposed than his struck him. His only real worry is political: that the time would be wasted, as he feels it was with climate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. Not because of me, I'd land on my feet, but because two years isn't enough to bring anyone with you. What would help is income support while people retrain and a law that says companies have to slow down cuts and fund training before they replace a crew.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd want robots to do, not just what they're scared of. Nobody in my crew wants to keep breathing vault fumes for the love of it; they want to keep their dignity and their paycheque. If you get those two right, most of the fear goes away.

headlineQuote: Nobody in my crew wants to keep breathing vault fumes for the love of it; they want to keep their dignity and their paycheque.
portrait: Carlos Young is a 43-year-old underground cable splicer and crew lead in a city's downtown vault network, married to a transit planner, with two children and a solid set of index funds. He's curious, generous and an early adopter who uses AI every day and built a chatbot for his apprentices. He's mildly disappointed by the hype scenario and sees gradual change as a chance to hand dangerous tasks to robots. Even with AGI in two years he's confident about himself, though anxious for colleagues and his children; with more time he becomes calm and plans to run robot crews and train others. He blames rushed decisions and weak policy, not the technology.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, not for himself but because two years isn't enough time to bring colleagues with him.
whatWouldHelp: Income support while people retrain and a law making companies slow down cuts and fund training before replacing a crew.
